title: Lamed
hookLine: the tallest letter; lamad means learn

cards: The room is loud. Not a library hush, the other kind. Long tables, big books open, and pairs of people leaning toward each other, arguing.
One reads a line aloud. The other says, wait, that can't be right, look at this word. Someone laughs.
Someone thumps the page. This is a beit midrash, a study hall, and the noise is the point: learning here is done out loud, in pairs, with someone who will push back.
Over the door you could hang a single letter, sticking up above all the others.

teach.b: First, look at it. The letters around it sit between two invisible lines. Lamed doesn't stay put: its neck rises above the top line, and teachers of the alef-bet call it the tallest letter.
A letter reaching for something higher. Second, listen to it. Lamed opens the verb for learning.
Lamad: he learned. Limed: he taught.

A student is a talmid, a teacher a melamed, and the great collection of the rabbis' discussions is the Talmud. Hear the same three letters, l, m, d, in each: the student, the teacher and the book. Third, the Torah.

When Moses gathers the people to repeat the commandments, in the King James he says: "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and judgments which I speak in your ears this day, that ye may learn them, and keep, and do them."
Learn, then keep, then do. Learning comes first in the line, and doing comes out of it. Fourth, how learning goes wrong.
In Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the sages, Hillel teaches that someone too shy to ask cannot learn, and someone too impatient cannot teach.
The student has to be willing to look foolish for a moment; the teacher has to be willing to explain it again. The tall letter isn't tall because it knows everything. It's reaching.
Every real question you ask is a little lamed, sticking up above the line.

how: In a beit midrash, a study hall, students may learn in pairs called chavruta, reading texts aloud and arguing over them; Torah study, talmud torah, is counted in Jewish tradition as a commandment in its own right.

games.q: you don't understand the line your study partner just read. everyone else seems to. what does Hillel's teaching in Pirkei Avot point you toward?
o: stay quiet so you don't look foolish.
ask, because the shy cannot learn.
skip ahead and hope it makes sense later.
games.why: Hillel teaches that the one too shy to ask cannot learn, and the one too impatient cannot teach.

practice: Bring to mind something you've been pretending to understand: a word you nod along to, how something works at your job, a prayer you've never looked up.
Name it plainly, I don't know this yet, let any embarrassment be there, and picture asking the question out loud, the way they do in the study hall. If you pray, ask for understanding.

wordCard.voice: Lamed. The tall letter, rising above the line, carrying the root of learning: lamad, talmid, Talmud. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: he learned. The letter lamed (ל) begins it; the same letters, l-m-d, run through talmid, student, and Talmud.

carryVoice: Your line: lamed learns. Asking out loud is how all learning starts. See you tomorrow.
